paragraphs.source_en: “He has no other vices to speak of, but he buys books in heaps, whether he reads them or not. If only he bought them after giving some thought to what he needed, it would be one thing; but he goes off to Maruzen without the least discrimination and comes back with any number of volumes, then when the end of the month arrives he acts as though nothing had happened. Take the end of last year, for instance: several months’ worth of book bills piled up unpaid, and it was perfectly dreadful.” “Oh, is that all? Books are the sort of thing one may as well let him buy if he wants them. There is no great harm in it. If they come to collect, all you need do is say, ‘I’ll pay soon, I’ll pay soon,’ and the collector will go away.” “Even so, one cannot go on putting them off forever.” The master’s wife said this with a discontented, gloomy air. “That is simple enough. Have him cut down his book expenses.” “As if it were so easy. He would never listen. Only the other day he said to me, ‘You are unfit to be the wife of a scholar; you have not the slightest understanding of the value of books. In ancient Rome there is a story of just this sort; for your instruction, I shall tell it to you.’” “How fascinating. What sort of story did he tell?” Meitei at once grew keenly interested. It was less out of sympathy for the master’s wife than from being driven by curiosity. “He said that long ago in Rome there was an emperor called ‘Tarkin’...” “Tarkin? That name Tarkin is rather odd.” “I cannot possibly remember those troublesome foreign names. They say he was the seventh emperor!” “Indeed, the seventh Emperor Tarkin? That is very amusing! Well then, go on. What happened to this seventh Tarkin?” “Oh, if even you are going to make fun of me, then I have no place to hide my face. If you know the proper name, would it not be better for you to teach me? How unkind you are!” The master’s wife turned sharply on Meitei. Meitei said, “Not at all. I would never laugh at you. I am not a man of such ill nature. I merely found your ‘seventh Tarkin’ rather striking... Well, let me think. You said the seventh Tarkin, did you not? Hmm, I do not remember it clearly, but I suppose you mean Tarquin the Proud. Well, whoever it was, that hardly matters. What, in the end, did this emperor do?” “They say a woman came to that emperor with nine books and asked him to buy them.” “I see!” “They say the emperor asked how much she wanted for them, and she named an extraordinarily high price. Since the emperor thought it too dear, he asked whether she could not lower it a little; whereupon the woman suddenly threw three of the nine books into the fire and burned them.” “What a pity.” “They say those books contained prophecies and such things, matters that could be found in no other books at all.” “Well!” “The emperor thought that, since the nine books had become six, she would surely ask somewhat less, and he asked what price she wanted for the six. But it was still the original price, not a single coin less. The emperor said this was outrageous, whereupon the woman again took up three books and threw them into the fire.

units.source_en: “He has no other vices to speak of, but he buys books in heaps, whether he reads them or not. If only he bought them after giving some thought to what he needed, it would be one thing; but he goes off to Maruzen without the least discrimination and comes back with any number of volumes, then when the end of the month arrives he acts as though nothing had happened.
